group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 31-year-old man was transferred by ambulance from the skilled nursing facility where he resides for assistance with activities of daily living after staff noted that, over the preceding 24 hours, a hacking productive cough, shaking chills, and feverish flushing had progressed to incoherent speech and failure to recognize familiar caregivers. His background is remarkable for a right middle cerebral artery infarction at age 28 that left mild spasticity of the left upper limb and limited his ability to live independently; he also carries a diagnosis of autoimmune cholangiopathy followed by hepatology with stable synthetic function and has never been told of chronic kidney impairment, malignancy, or cardiac pump failure. He uses no tobacco, drinks only at holiday meals, and denies non-prescribed drug exposure. Facility nurses withheld antipyretics, antibiotics, bronchodilators, intravenous fluids, or supplemental oxygen prior to transport so that emergency staff could observe untreated physiology. On arrival he sat slumped on the gurney, pupils equal and brisk, but he answered questions with rambling phrases, misstated the month, and could not follow a two-step command, although motor strength appeared symmetric when prompted. Skin was hot, flushed, and lightly diaphoretic; oral mucosae were tacky. Pre-intervention vitals obtained in ambient air at sea-level recorded an oral temperature of 101.9 °F, regular but pronounced tachycardia at 136 beats per minute, automated blood pressure 143/78 mm Hg confirmed manually, rapid respirations at 45 breaths per minute with shallow excursions yet no use of accessory neck musculature, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 96 % and 98 %. Jugular venous contour was not elevated, and no peripheral edema or sacral swelling was present. Cardiac auscultation revealed a sharp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower posterior field and scattered rhonchi elsewhere; percussion remained resonant throughout, and no dull stony note suggested fluid layering. The abdomen was soft and nondistended; a smooth, mildly tender liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the costal margin without ascites or splenomegaly. No lower-extremity clubbing or cyanosis was observed. Capillary glucose performed before venipuncture measured 155 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of triage—before any saline flushes—revealed sodium 112 mEq/L, potassium 3.4 mEq/L, chloride 82 mEq/L, bicarbonate 28 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 63 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, the latter consistent with prior facility records, suggesting prerenal concentration rather than intrinsic nephropathy. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 14.8 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilic predominance, hematocrit 52 %, hemoglobin 17.3 g/dL, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. A radial arterial sample obtained while the patient continued on room air demonstrated a profound respiratory alkalosis with pH 7.70, PaCO₂ 23 mm Hg, PaO₂ 101 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 28 mEq/L. Serum lactate measured 1.4 mmol/L. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 138 beats per minute with a normal axis and no acute ischemic changes. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph, captured before any medication was administered, showed a dense patchy opacity filling the posterior segment of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, preserved costophrenic angles, and no blunting or meniscus to suggest free pleural fluid; cardiomediastinal silhouette and mediastinal contour were unremarkable. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, expectorated sputum for Gram stain and culture, urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory prior to any antimicrobial, antipyretic, intravenous fluid, or oxygen orders. At the time of this documentation he remains seated upright breathing ambient air, has not received crystalloid or vasoactive agents, and his physiologic observations, laboratory data, and imaging findings above represent his untreated presentation state.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) uses the untreated admission findings.
1. Demographics: A man starts with his age in points (31). Skilled nursing facility residence adds 10. Subtotal: 41.
2. Comorbidities: Chronic liver disease (autoimmune cholangiopathy) adds 20; cerebrovascular disease (prior MCA infarct) adds 10. No malignancy, heart failure, or chronic renal disease is reported (0 each). Subtotal: 30.
3. Examination: Acute disorientation adds 20; respiratory rate 45/min (≥30) adds 20; pulse 136/min (≥125) adds 10. Systolic pressure 143 mm Hg is not <90 (0), and temperature 38.8°C is neither <35 nor ≥40 (0). Subtotal: 50.
4. Tests: BUN 63 mg/dL (≥30) adds 20 and sodium 112 mEq/L (<130) adds 20. Arterial pH 7.70 is not <7.35; glucose 155 mg/dL is not ≥250; hematocrit 52% is not <30%; room-air PaO₂ 101 mm Hg is not <60; and there is no pleural effusion (0 each). Subtotal: 40.
PSI = 41 + 30 + 50 + 40 = 161.
Final answer: 161
